President, my delegation remains convinced that the fight against terrorism will not have impact without strengthening international legal cooperation. Perpetrators, commanders and those who support terrorist acts must be held accountable, given that the victims must also have access to justice, fully respecting the principles of the rule of law. In this connection, the DRC believes that it would be desirable that the international community continue its efforts to have a legal universally accepted definition of terrorism. This step forward would make a contribution to strengthening legal security, would facilitate international cooperation, and it would consolidate the fight against impunity. Moreover, The sanctions regime created by the resolutions 1267 and 2553 remains an important instrument in the fight against terrorist networks. It is effective because it is rigorous, impartial and consistent in how it is implemented by all Member States, and it is based on objective criteria that are regularly updated. President no state, whatever means they have can address this challenge alone because the ramifications go beyond borders and beyond continents. This is why the DRC reaffirms its full support to the UN Global Counterterrorism Strategy and the Global Coordination Compact, as well as the ongoing efforts carried out by the UNOCT and CTED. that seek to strengthen and build member states capacity in the long term. Our collective action must remain guided by the purposes and principles of the UN Charter, respect for state sovereignty, the rule of law, international law, international human rights law and international humanitarian law. President, to conclude, the Democratic Republic of the Congo reiterates its unequivocal condemnation of terrorism in all its forms and manifestations, wherever it takes place, whenever it happens or whoever carries it out. We remain convinced that the response to this threat should not be exclusively a security one. While military responses crucial, it will only be possible in the long term if resolute action is taken to strengthen the rule of law, good governance, development, prevention of violent extremism, and if efforts are made for international cooperation. When faced with an ever-changing threat, only a global, multilateral response based on solidarity between States and respecting international law will address the root causes in the long term. Only that will protect civilians and preserve and maintain international peace and security. Thank you.
Thank you, Representative of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, for the statement, and I give the floor to the representative of Colombia.

Thank you very much. Madam President, I wish to begin by congratulating Denmark on assuming the presidency of the Security Council. I wish them every success in that role, and I wish to thank them for convening today's meeting. I'd also like to take this opportunity to congratulate and thank the Democratic Republic of the Congo for their presidency in July. Allow me also, Madam President, to convey our condolences to the government of Pakistan following the attack there. I thank the Secretary General for his report and Ms. Niyazberdieva and Muskenov for their briefings. Madam President, while it is clear from the report that progress has been made, our work is far from over. Terrorism continues to stand as one of the main threats to international peace and security. It undermines the rule of law, destabilises states and wreaks suffering on a major scale. Colombia reaffirms its condemnation of terrorism in all its forms and manifestations and wherever and by whomever terrorist acts may be committed. In connection with the report, allow me to make five points. One, in spite of its territorial losses and leadership setbacks, the Islamic State of Iraq and the Levant continues to pose a threat to international peace and security in view of its resilience, its adaptability and its constantly evolving tactics. Colombia reiterates that the fight against this scourge must focus on making it less ideologically attractive. This fight must also focus on tackling factors driving radicalisation and on prevention. It must also pre-empt both traditional and emerging threats. My second point, we agree with the report's emphasis on the need for greater coordination and cooperation to combat the terrorist threat. We particularly welcome the roadmap that was adopted by the UN Global Counter-Terrorism Coordination Compact. We also are of the view that it is crucial to ensure close cooperation with the African Union and with Central Asian states. and international pressure must be unified and continue to be brought to bear. There is an urgent need to continue capacity building, and this is my third point. In this connection, we are grateful for the efforts of the committee and its field visits to support states to improve their capacity and infrastructures. They have also worked to help effective implementation of the global counter-terrorism strategy and the relevant resolutions of the Security Council. Here, we reiterate the importance of ensuring that building activities bear in mind regional and local contexts. These activities must be tailored to the needs and priorities of beneficiary states and this includes activities designed to harness the preventive potential of technologies such as AI and unmanned aerial vehicles. These efforts avoid that these technologies and systems being used by terrorists. Our fourth point, we continue to be concerned by the situation of children previously associated with terrorist groups. They must be reintegrated into civilian life and their recruitment must be prevented through the comprehensive implementation of Security Council resolutions on children and armed conflicts and more specifically the implementation of 2427. Here we must continue to forge ahead with the WPS agenda and it must be fully incorporated into the fight against terrorism based on the provisions of resolutions 2242 and 2467. My fifth point, we support the sanctions committees 1267, 1989 and 2253 and we appeal for a review of the list of persons and entities designated by these committees because the report details countless acts that have been perpetrated by people that are not under sanction. We reiterate our full commitment to the renewed GCTS and we support the UNOCT, CTED, the UN Global Counterterrorism Coordination Compact and the 1267 Monitoring Team. We encourage all of the above entities to bolster internal and inter-institutional cooperation and to continue to hold productive dialogue with the UN membership and with this Council. Allow me to conclude by noting that the fight against terrorism can only be successful if it is underpinned by an approach of coordination and one that fully focuses on human rights. It's only in that way that we can win the battle long term.

Representative of Colombia for the statement. And I shall now make a statement in my capacity as the representative of Denmark. I thank the briefers for their presentations and the Secretary-General for his 23rd report on the threat posed by ISIL or Daesh to international peace and security. As we have heard, the threat posed by Daesh persists and is becoming increasingly diverse. In a year where we are commemorating the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 attacks, The international community's fights against terrorism remains crucial. I'll make three points. First, under Sahel, Denmark condemns the terrorist attacks carried out in the region and the continued violations of international humanitarian law. The countries of the region must urgently strengthen cross-border cooperation, protect civilians, support humanitarian access, and address governance deficits, which can be exploited by terrorist groups. Counterterrorism operations must always comply with international law. Preventive action is the most effective solution. Counterterrorism operations should be accompanied by good governance, basic services, and engagement with local communities. Cross-border initiatives and regional collaboration are essential in preventing and countering terrorism. We must continue to build on African-led efforts as part of strengthening the region's collective security response. UNOWAS, in close partnership with regional actors such as the African Union and ECOWAS, can also support efforts towards a conducive political environment for enhanced security cooperation. Second, on Syria. We commend Syria for the strengthened efforts in combating terrorism and urge further action to address the threat comprehensively as a member of the counter-Daesh coalition. However, prison escapes and a large number of former detainees and camp residents who have remained unaccounted for have created serious risk of renewed recruitment and mobilization. Last month, terrorist attacks in Damascus serve as a reminder of the importance of sustained counterterrorism pressure. Following the closure of the al-Hol camp, we stressed that individuals affiliated with Daesh must be addressed through lawful and predictable frameworks, including prosecutions where appropriate. Moreover, the closure has led to a more tenuous position for many children and more should be done to protect them. Third, multilateral cooperation remains indispensable. The global counter-terrorism strategy provides a shared framework and must be implemented in a balanced manner across all four pillars, with human rights and the rule of law at its core. This includes strengthened cooperation to address the misuse of emerging technologies such as AI, digital platforms and virtual assets. The 1267 sanctions regime must remain up to date, credible and responsive. As a former, and hopefully future, Chair of the Committee, Denmark regrets that not all key figures of listed terrorist groups are themselves listed. Denmark has submitted a proposal to expand the list, and we hope that they will be added without further delay. We remind all states of their obligation to implement the sanctions fully and urge them to support the monitoring team with timely, detailed information. I thank you, and I resume my function as President of the Council. There are no more names inscribed on the list of speakers. The meeting is adjourned.
